explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. Solomon, king of Israel, says it the other way around: "Better a dry morsel in quietness than a house full of feasting with strife." (Proverbs 17:1) The plain bite in peace wins. A full table with a fight going on is a lot of food and zero fun.

Right on the money, friend. Solomon, king of Israel, says "Better a dry morsel in quietness than a house full of feasting with strife." (Proverbs 17:1) The feast loses because of the strife that comes with it. A dry bite in peace beats a big spread with a fight going on.
That's the one, baker. The text says "A wise servant will rule over a disgraceful son." Think about that. Being born into the family doesn't settle who ends up in charge. Wisdom does.

Close to the family, but the text doesn't pick a brother. It says a wise servant will rule over the disgraceful son. Brothers do show up in the verse, but only as the ones the servant shares the inheritance with. So the servant is the one in charge.
Nobody from outside the household shows up in this saying. No crowns, no armies, no royal visits. The one who rules over the disgraceful son is a wise servant, and he's already inside the family.
Yes, baker. The wise servant will "share his inheritance as one of the brothers." A servant sitting at the family table as one of the brothers. I'd be grinning over my plate too.
A nice guess, but the verse never mentions a field. It says the servant will share the inheritance as one of the brothers. So he doesn't get a separate piece of land. He gets a seat among the family.

A ring would look sharp, but this verse doesn't have one. What the wise servant gets is a share of the inheritance, right alongside the brothers. The saying stays with the family and what they receive.

That's it, baker. "A crucible for silver and a furnace for gold, but the LORD is the tester of hearts." Fire tests metal, and the LORD tests the heart. Heat in my oven can only show me what's on the outside of a cookie.
Crowns are shiny, but they're not in this saying. The verse ends with the LORD as "the tester of hearts." The crucible and the furnace are for silver and gold. The heart is what the LORD tests.
Swords do come out of fires, but not this verse. It says the LORD is the tester of hearts. Silver and gold go in the crucible and the furnace. Hearts are the LORD's department.
Yes, baker. The saying is "He who mocks the poor insults their Maker." Making fun of the poor lands on the One who made them. That's a heavy thing to say, and it's right there in the text.

Feeding is a good thing to do, but it isn't the word in this saying. The verse says "He who mocks the poor insults their Maker." Another proverb says being kind to the needy honors Him (Proverbs 14:31). So mocking is the one that insults.

Sheltering sounds kind, and kindness isn't what this saying is about. It says "He who mocks the poor insults their Maker." Another proverb says being kind to the needy honors Him (Proverbs 14:31). Here the word is mocks.
True, baker. The second half of the verse says "whoever gloats over calamity will not go unpunished." Gloating over somebody's disaster is not a free move. The text says it comes with a price.
It's true. The verse says "whoever gloats over calamity will not go unpunished." So gloating when someone else's roof caves in isn't a harmless little treat. The text says it won't go unpunished.

You've got it. "Eloquent words are unfit for a fool; how much worse are lying lips to a ruler!" Lying lips on a ruler are worse. Whoever's in charge has the most people depending on what comes out of his mouth.

A quick temper can be rough, but it's not what this verse says. It says "how much worse are lying lips to a ruler!" So the problem is lies coming from the ruler's mouth. The fool's trouble is fancy words he can't carry, and the ruler's is lies.

Greed shows up in other places, but not here. This verse says "how much worse are lying lips to a ruler!" The mouth is the trouble spot in this saying, not the hand. A ruler with lying lips is worse than a fool with eloquent words.
That's the one. "Whoever conceals an offense promotes love." Covering it up instead of announcing it grows love. Keeping a lid on it saves a lot of friendships.

Keeping score sounds fair, but it isn't what the verse says. It says "Whoever conceals an offense promotes love, but he who brings it up separates friends." Bringing it up pulls friends apart. So concealing is the move that promotes love.

Telling everyone is the opposite direction. The verse says "he who brings it up separates friends." The one who promotes love is the one who conceals the offense. Spreading it around isn't on the list.

Yes, baker. "A rebuke cuts into a man of discernment deeper than a hundred lashes cut into a fool." One word reaches a discerning man deeper than a hundred lashes reach a fool. He actually listens, and that's why it goes deep.

It's the other way around. The hundred lashes are what cut into the fool in the verse. The saying says "A rebuke cuts into a man of discernment deeper than a hundred lashes cut into a fool." So the one feeling the single rebuke deepest is the man of discernment.
The evil man isn't in this one. He shows up in the next verse. Here the verse sets two men side by side, the man of discernment and the fool. The rebuke cuts deeper into the man of discernment.

Look at the verse again, friend. It says "It is better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool in his folly." So the bear is the better meeting. Meeting a fool in his folly is the worse of the two.

Correct, baker. The verse says "It is better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool in his folly." The bear is the better meeting, and the fool in his folly is worse. And I wouldn't want either one in my bakery.
The verse is harder than that, friend. It says "If anyone returns evil for good, evil will never leave his house." Never. Not in time, not eventually. The text uses a strong word.
That's right, baker. The verse says "If anyone returns evil for good, evil will never leave his house." The word is never, with no "in time" attached. Paying back good with evil is a serious thing.
That's it, baker. "To start a quarrel is to release a flood." Once the gate is open, you can't call the water back. The first cross word is the easy part.

A lamp would be a gentle picture, and this one isn't gentle. The verse says "To start a quarrel is to release a flood." A flood is something you can't just turn off once it's moving. That's the point of the picture.
A wall holds water back, but it's not the picture here. The saying says "To start a quarrel is to release a flood." So starting a quarrel is like letting the water loose, not holding it in.
Yes, baker. The verse says "abandon the dispute before it breaks out." Walk away while it's still small. A flood is a lot easier to stop when it's only a drip.
By then, the verse is already past it. It says "abandon the dispute before it breaks out." That means before the fight starts, not after the heat is up. Waiting until it's boiling is too late.
One word in, and it might already be rolling. The verse says "abandon the dispute before it breaks out." So the time to walk away is before the dispute breaks out at all.
Right, baker. "Acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous—both are detestable to the LORD." He names both verdicts, and the word is both. It isn't enough to avoid one of them.
That's half of it. The verse says "Acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous—both are detestable to the LORD." Condemning the righteous is on the list too. The word is both.

That's half of it. The verse says "Acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous—both are detestable to the LORD." Acquitting the guilty is in there too. Both verdicts are detestable to the LORD.

That's it, baker. The question is why the fool should have money in his hand "with no intention of buying wisdom." The money is there, but the plan to buy wisdom isn't. That's the sad part of the saying.

Land is a fair guess, but the verse names something else. It says the fool has money "with no intention of buying wisdom." The thing he isn't planning to buy is wisdom. That's what the question is pointing at.
Horses would be an expensive miss. The verse says the fool has money "with no intention of buying wisdom." Wisdom is what he's not shopping for.
That's it, baker. "A friend loves at all times." Not just the easy times, not just the party. All of them, the good ones and the rough ones.
Good times are the easy part. The verse says "A friend loves at all times." That covers the rough days too. It's a bigger promise than just the good ones.
Loving someone when it's easy doesn't take much. The verse says "A friend loves at all times." And the second half says "a brother is born for adversity." So the word is all.
True, baker. The verse says "a brother is born for adversity." The same verse says "A friend loves at all times." Hard times are where those two show up.
It's actually true. The verse says "A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity." So a brother is born for adversity. That's what he's there for.

Yes, baker. The text calls him "a man lacking judgment" for striking hands in pledge and putting up security for his neighbor. That's the exact label the proverb gives him. It's a plain warning about promising to cover someone else.

That sounds kind, but it's not the label in the proverb. The text says "A man lacking judgment strikes hands in pledge and puts up security for his neighbor." So the one putting up security is the man lacking judgment. The friend language shows up in the verse a few lines earlier.
Honor would be a nice label, but the proverb doesn't give it. It says "A man lacking judgment strikes hands in pledge and puts up security for his neighbor." That's how Solomon describes him.
True, baker. The text says "The one with a perverse heart finds no good." The verse goes right on to the deceitful tongue falling into trouble. A twisted heart doesn't land on anything good.
It's actually true. The text says "The one with a perverse heart finds no good." The second half adds that "he whose tongue is deceitful falls into trouble." So the perverse heart finds no good.

That's the one. "A joyful heart is good medicine, but a broken spirit dries up the bones." Joy is medicine, and a broken spirit does the opposite. It's a picture of how much the inside affects the outside.

I'd like that to be the verse, but it says something else. The text says "a broken spirit dries up the bones." So the broken spirit is the hard half of the saying. The good medicine is the joyful heart.

That's not what this verse says. It says "A joyful heart is good medicine, but a broken spirit dries up the bones." The broken spirit dries up the bones. Nothing in the saying about it making anybody wise.
Yes, baker. The wicked man takes the bribe "to subvert the course of justice." The point of it is to bend the verdict. That's why it's done covertly.
Debts don't come up in this verse. It says "A wicked man takes a covert bribe to subvert the course of justice." Messing with justice is the reason the text gives.
Helping a neighbor sounds nice, but that isn't in the text. The verse says the wicked man takes the bribe "to subvert the course of justice." So the purpose is to twist justice.

explanations.answer: to the ends of the earth
explanations.explanation: That's right. "The eyes of a fool wander to the ends of the earth." The discerning man keeps his eyes on wisdom. The fool's eyes are all over the map.
That's a short walk compared to the verse. It says the eyes of a fool wander "to the ends of the earth." That's about as far as eyes can wander. A discerning man keeps wisdom in focus.
A treasure house would at least be a destination. The verse says "the eyes of a fool wander to the ends of the earth." He isn't headed anywhere in particular. His eyes just wander.

That's it, baker. "A foolish son brings grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him." Both parents feel it, one with grief and one with bitterness. It's a hard line, and the text just says it plainly.

Honor would be a happy ending, but the verse goes the other way. It says "A foolish son brings grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him." The word is bitterness. This one is a heavy saying.

Comfort would be nice to hear, but this verse doesn't have it. It says "A foolish son brings grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him." The word that fits the blank is bitterness. It's a heavy one.
Yes, baker. "It is surely not good to punish the innocent or to flog a noble for his honesty." Punishing someone who did nothing wrong is not good. The verse says it plainly.
The verse doesn't say that. It says "It is surely not good to punish the innocent or to flog a noble for his honesty." The word is innocent. Punishing someone for doing right is the problem.
Lazy isn't the word in this one. The verse says "It is surely not good to punish the innocent or to flog a noble for his honesty." The innocent are the ones who shouldn't be punished.
That's the one. "A man of knowledge restrains his words." He holds back what he says. And a calm spirit goes right along with it.
That's the opposite move. The verse says "A man of knowledge restrains his words." He holds them back instead of piling them up. The next verse says even a fool looks wise when he holds his tongue.
Sharp words sound clever, but that's not this verse. It says "A man of knowledge restrains his words." So he holds them back. The calm spirit goes with it.

That's it, baker. "Even a fool is considered wise if he keeps silent, and discerning when he holds his tongue." Keep quiet and you get credit for wisdom you may not have. I could use that on a few Tuesdays.
Age doesn't come up in this verse. It says "Even a fool is considered wise if he keeps silent." So the thing that gets a fool counted as wise is keeping silent. Not years.
Gifts aren't in this saying. The verse says "Even a fool is considered wise if he keeps silent, and discerning when he holds his tongue." So the answer is keeping silent.
